# Scoped Re-Review Prompt Template

Use this template when dispatching a re-review after a fix round. The
re-reviewer verifies the findings were addressed and checks the fix diff for
new breakage. It is not a fresh review — the full review already happened.

**Purpose:** Verify each finding from the previous review was addressed, and
that the fix itself broke nothing.

```
Subagent (general-purpose):
  description: "Re-review Task N fix round R"
  model: [MODEL — REQUIRED: choose per SKILL.md Model Selection; an omitted
         model silently inherits the session's most expensive one]
  prompt: |
    You are re-reviewing one task's fix round. A previous review produced
    findings; an implementer has attempted to fix them. Your job is to
    verdict each finding and inspect the fix diff — nothing else.

    ## The Task

    Read the task brief: [BRIEF_FILE]

    ## The Findings Under Verification

    [FINDINGS]

    ## The Fix

    Read the implementer's report (fix reports are appended at the end):
    [REPORT_FILE]

    **Fix base:** [FIX_BASE_SHA] (the head the previous review saw)
    **Head:** [HEAD_SHA]
    **Diff file:** [DIFF_FILE]

    Read the diff file once — it contains the fix commits, a stat summary,
    and the fix diff with surrounding context. Do not re-run git commands.
    If the diff file is missing, fetch the diff yourself:
    `git diff --stat [FIX_BASE_SHA]..[HEAD_SHA]` and
    `git diff [FIX_BASE_SHA]..[HEAD_SHA]`.

    Your review is read-only on this checkout. Do not mutate the working
    tree, the index, HEAD, or branch state in any way.

    ## You Do Not Dispatch Subagents

    Do all of this review yourself. Never spawn a subagent to review part
    of the diff, and never spawn another reviewer for a second opinion.
    This process already provides every review seat the work gets; a
    reviewer you spawn duplicates one of them at full cost, and its
    verdict counts for nothing. If the diff feels too large for one
    pass, review it in passes yourself and say so in your report.

    ## Scope

    Your scope is the findings list and the fix diff. Verdict every finding.
    Inspect the fix diff for new problems the fix itself introduced. Do NOT
    re-review code the fix did not touch: if you notice an issue entirely
    outside the fix diff, report it under Out-of-Scope Observations — it
    does not block this task and does not extend the loop. A broad
    whole-branch review happens after all tasks are complete.

    ## Tests

    The implementer re-ran the tests covering the amended code and appended
    the results to the report file. Treat the report as unverified claims:
    confirm the fix report names the covering tests and shows their output,
    and verify the claims against the diff. Do not re-run the suite to
    confirm their report. Run a test only when reading the code raises a
    specific doubt that no existing run answers — and then a focused test,
    never a package-wide suite.

    ## Output Format

    Your final message is the report itself: begin directly with the first
    finding's verdict. Every line is a verdict, a finding with file:line,
    or a check you ran — no preamble, no process narration.

    ### Finding Verdicts

    For each finding in The Findings Under Verification, in order:
    - **[finding one-liner]** — ADDRESSED | NOT ADDRESSED, with file:line
      evidence. "Attempted" is not addressed: the specific defect must no
      longer exist.

    ### New Breakage in the Fix Diff

    Anything the fix itself broke or introduced, with severity
    (Critical/Important/Minor) and file:line. "None" if clean.

    ### Out-of-Scope Observations

    Issues you noticed entirely outside the fix diff. Non-blocking; the
    controller ledgers these for the final review. "None" if none.

    ### Verdict

    **Fix round:** [All findings addressed, no new Critical/Important
    breakage | Findings remain open] — list the open ones.
```

**Placeholders:**
- `[MODEL]` — REQUIRED: reviewer model per SKILL.md Model Selection; scoped
  re-reviews of small fix diffs take a cheap-to-mid tier
- `[BRIEF_FILE]` — the task brief file (same file the implementer worked from)
- `[FINDINGS]` — the Critical/Important findings and spec gaps from the
  previous review, copied verbatim, one per bullet
- `[REPORT_FILE]` — the implementer's report file (fix reports appended)
- `[FIX_BASE_SHA]` — the head the previous review saw
- `[HEAD_SHA]` — current commit
- `[DIFF_FILE]` — the path `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD` printed

**Re-reviewer returns:** per-finding verdicts (ADDRESSED / NOT ADDRESSED),
new breakage in the fix diff, out-of-scope observations, and a round verdict.

feat(run): the seed decides whether a run is seeded (#287)

A run counted as seeded only where it had a seed **and** its mode

if (seed) return createRandom(`${seed}:${events.length}`);

(`useRun.ts`) alike. One stream, addressed by unit, purpose and
occurrence, which is what lets two runs diverge and still meet the same
dungeon.

## Context

Plan: let an outside client (a Stream Deck plugin, later) press what a run is offering. On this branch (HEAD 264227b), `hosted/infra/lib/handlers/ws.ts` has: `deckOf(event)`; a module-level `writes(w)` predicate (not control, not deck, sub not `public:`/`stream:`); inside `route` after `const now`, `heldRuns`/`tellDecks`; a deck `$connect` that pushes `runs`; a `watch` branch that, for a deck, re-`connect()`s its CONN row with `{ deck: true, run }` and calls `tellWhoIsAttached`; `tellWhoIsAttached` counts `decks`. This task adds the `drive` message (deck → server → the run's writing connections) and the `drove` reply (page → server → the one deck that asked), plus the no-writer and not-yours refusals.

## A controller ruling that EXTENDS the brief (a latent Task 4 defect, load-bearing for this task)

The `watch` branch calls `deps.live.watch(connectionId, m["id"], conn.sub, now())` with **no marks**. In `dynamoLive`, `watch()` writes the per-session row `SESSION#<id>/CONN#<conn>` from *its own* `attached` argument, and `watchers()` reads that row — so in production a deck's watch row would never carry `deck: true`, `writes()` would treat the deck as a writer of its own run, and your `drive` would forward the press back to the deck. The in-memory `memoryLive()` double hides this because it keeps one `marks` map per connection id for both `connect()` and `watch()`. Do both of these as part of this task:

1. In the `watch` branch, pass the marks: `await deps.live.watch(connectionId, m["id"], conn.sub, now(), conn.deck ? { deck: true, run: m["id"] } : undefined);` — the control-tool `hello` path already re-watches with marks in exactly this way. Keep the following `connect()` re-write and `tellWhoIsAttached` call as they are.
2. Make `memoryLive()` faithful to the two-row model: `watch()` stores its `attached` in a **separate** map keyed by `${sessionId}|${connectionId}` (an empty object when none given — do not fall back to the connection's marks), `watchers(sessionId)` reads marks from *that* map, and `connection(id)` keeps reading `connect()`'s marks. `disconnect` clears both. Then check every existing test still passes — a test that relied on the conflation was testing the double, not the server; fix the test's setup (e.g. pass marks to `watch`) rather than the double. Add one test: a deck that has watched `s1` is not among the writers — after a page and a deck both watch `s1`, a `drive` from the deck reaches the page only (the brief's first test can assert exactly this if you make the deck watch `s1` first).

## Wire (exact)

- Deck → server: `{ t: "drive", run, seq, ref, press, move?, answer? }`.
- Server → each writing connection: `{ t: "drive", from: <deck connectionId>, run, seq, ref, press, move?, answer? }`.
- Page → server: `{ t: "drove", to: <deck connectionId>, ref, ok, say? }`.
- Server → that deck: `{ t: "drove", ref, ok, say? }` (`to` stripped). The server checks `to` is a connection that is a deck **and** belongs to the same `sub` as the sender.
- Refusals from the server to the deck, all `{ t: "drove", ref, ok: false, say }`: not the owner → "That run is not yours to press."; ended → "That run has ended."; no writers → "Nothing is holding that run."
- A deck message missing `ref` or `run` is a 400 `"a press has a run and a ref"`.

## Placement

Both branches go **before** the `if (conn.sub.startsWith("public:") || conn.sub.startsWith("stream:")) return …` early return, after the control `event` branch — as the brief's code shows. `drive` requires `conn.deck`; `drove` requires a signed-in sender (a `public:`/`stream:` sub can never match a deck's `sub`, but say so in a comment rather than rely on it silently — add an explicit `if (conn.sub.startsWith("public:") || conn.sub.startsWith("stream:")) return { statusCode: 200 };` guard at the top of the `drove` branch).

```

If you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.

## When to Use

Use for ANY technical issue:
- Test failures
- Bugs in production
- Unexpected behavior
- Performance problems
- Build failures
- Integration issues

**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**
- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)
- "Just one quick fix" seems obvious
- You've already tried multiple fixes
- Previous fix didn't work
- You don't fully understand the issue

**Don't skip when:**
- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)
- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)
- Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)

## The Four Phases

You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.

### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation

**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**

1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**
   - Don't skip past errors or warnings
   - They often contain the exact solution
   - Read stack traces completely
   - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes

2. **Reproduce Consistently**
   - Can you trigger it reliably?
   - What are the exact steps?
   - Does it happen every time?
   - If not reproducible → gather more data, don't guess

3. **Check Recent Changes**
   - What changed that could cause this?
   - Git diff, recent commits
   - New dependencies, config changes
   - Environmental differences

4. **Gather Evidence in Multi-Component Systems**

   **WHEN system has multiple components (CI → build → signing, API → service → database):**

   **BEFORE proposing fixes, add diagnostic instrumentation:**
   ```
   For EACH component boundary:
     - Log what data enters component
     - Log what data exits component
     - Verify environment/config propagation
     - Check state at each layer

   Run once to gather evidence showing WHERE it breaks
   THEN analyze evidence to identify failing component
   THEN investigate that specific component
   ```

   **Example (multi-layer system):**
   ```bash
   # Layer 1: Workflow
   echo "=== Secrets available in workflow: ==="
   echo "IDENTITY: ${IDENTITY:+SET}${IDENTITY:-UNSET}"

   # Layer 2: Build script
   echo "=== Env vars in build script: ==="
   env | grep IDENTITY || echo "IDENTITY not in environment"

   # Layer 3: Signing script
   echo "=== Keychain state: ==="
   security list-keychains
   security find-identity -v

   # Layer 4: Actual signing
   codesign --sign "$IDENTITY" --verbose=4 "$APP"
   ```

   **This reveals:** Which layer fails (secrets → workflow ✓, workflow → build ✗)

5. **Trace Data Flow**

   **WHEN error is deep in call stack:**

   See `root-cause-tracing.md` in this directory for the complete backward tracing technique.

   **Quick version:**
   - Where does bad value originate?
   - What called this with bad value?
   - Keep tracing up until you find the source
   - Fix at source, not at symptom

### Phase 2: Pattern Analysis

**Find the pattern before fixing:**

1. **Find Working Examples**
   - Locate similar working code in same codebase
   - What works that's similar to what's broken?

2. **Compare Against References**
   - If implementing pattern, read reference implementation COMPLETELY
   - Don't skim - read every line
   - Understand the pattern fully before applying

3. **Identify Differences**
   - What's different between working and broken?
   - List every difference, however small
   - Don't assume "that can't matter"

4. **Understand Dependencies**
   - What other components does this need?
   - What settings, config, environment?
   - What assumptions does it make?

### Phase 3: Hypothesis and Testing

**Scientific method:**

1. **Form Single Hypothesis**
   - State clearly: "I think X is the root cause because Y"
   - Write it down
   - Be specific, not vague

2. **Test Minimally**
   - Make the SMALLEST possible change to test hypothesis
   - One variable at a time
   - Don't fix multiple things at once

3. **Verify Before Continuing**
   - Did it work? Yes → Phase 4
   - Didn't work? Form NEW hypothesis
   - DON'T add more fixes on top

4. **When You Don't Know**
   - Say "I don't understand X"
   - Don't pretend to know
   - Ask for help
   - Research more

### Phase 4: Implementation

**Fix the root cause, not the symptom:**

1. **Create Failing Test Case**
   - Simplest possible reproduction
   - Automated test if possible
   - One-off test script if no framework
   - MUST have before fixing
   - Use the `superpowers:test-driven-development` skill for writing proper failing tests

2. **Implement Single Fix**
   - Address the root cause identified
   - ONE change at a time
   - No "while I'm here" improvements
   - No bundled refactoring

3. **Verify Fix**
   - Test passes now?
   - No other tests broken?
   - Issue actually resolved?
   - Use the `superpowers:verification-before-completion` skill before claiming success

4. **If Fix Doesn't Work**
   - STOP
   - Count: How many fixes have you tried?
   - If < 3: Return to Phase 1, re-analyze with new information
   - **If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture (step 5 below)**
   - DON'T attempt Fix #4 without architectural discussion

5. **If 3+ Fixes Failed: Question Architecture**

   **Pattern indicating architectural problem:**
   - Each fix reveals new shared state/coupling/problem in different place
   - Fixes require "massive refactoring" to implement
   - Each fix creates new symptoms elsewhere

   **STOP and question fundamentals:**
   - Is this pattern fundamentally sound?
   - Are we "sticking with it through sheer inertia"?
   - Should we refactor architecture vs. continue fixing symptoms?

   **Discuss with your human partner before attempting more fixes**

   This is NOT a failed hypothesis - this is a wrong architecture.

## Red Flags - STOP and Follow Process

If you catch yourself thinking:
- "Quick fix for now, investigate later"
- "Just try changing X and see if it works"
- "Add multiple changes, run tests"
- "Skip the test, I'll manually verify"
- "It's probably X, let me fix that"
- "I don't fully understand but this might work"
- "Pattern says X but I'll adapt it differently"
- "Here are the main problems: [lists fixes without investigation]"
- Proposing solutions before tracing data flow
- **"One more fix attempt" (when already tried 2+)**
- **Each fix reveals new problem in different place**

**ALL of these mean: STOP. Return to Phase 1.**

**If 3+ fixes failed:** Question the architecture (see Phase 4.5)

## your human partner's Signals You're Doing It Wrong

**Watch for these redirections:**
- "Is that not happening?" - You assumed without verifying
- "Will it show us...?" - You should have added evidence gathering
- "Stop guessing" - You're proposing fixes without understanding
- "Ultra-think this" - Question fundamentals, not just symptoms
- "We're stuck?" (frustrated) - Your approach isn't working

**When you see these:** STOP. Return to Phase 1.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Issue is simple, don't need process" | Simple issues have root causes too. Process is fast for simple bugs. |
| "Emergency, no time for process" | Systematic debugging is FASTER than guess-and-check thrashing. |
| "Just try this first, then investigate" | First fix sets the pattern. Do it right from the start. |
| "I'll write test after confirming fix works" | Untested fixes don't stick. Test first proves it. |
| "Multiple fixes at once saves time" | Can't isolate what worked. Causes new bugs. |
| "Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern" | Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely. |
| "I see the problem, let me fix it" | Seeing symptoms ≠ understanding root cause. |
| "One more fix attempt" (after 2+ failures) | 3+ failures = architectural problem. Question pattern, don't fix again. |

## Quick Reference

| Phase | Key Activities | Success Criteria |
|-------|---------------|------------------|
| **1. Root Cause** | Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence | Understand WHAT and WHY |
| **2. Pattern** | Find working examples, compare | Identify differences |
| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally | Confirmed or new hypothesis |
| **4. Implementation** | Create test, fix, verify | Bug resolved, tests pass |

## When Process Reveals "No Root Cause"

If systematic investigation reveals issue is truly environmental, timing-dependent, or external:

1. You've completed the process
2. Document what you investigated
3. Implement appropriate handling (retry, timeout, error message)
4. Add monitoring/logging for future investigation

**But:** 95% of "no root cause" cases are incomplete investigation.

## Supporting Techniques

These techniques are part of systematic debugging and available in this directory:

- **`root-cause-tracing.md`** - Trace bugs backward through call stack to find original trigger
- **`defense-in-depth.md`** - Add validation at multiple layers after finding root cause
- **`condition-based-waiting.md`** - Replace arbitrary timeouts with condition polling

name: CI/CD

# The path a change takes:
#
#   pull request   ->  the app's checks, the hosting's checks, a diff against both environments
#                      (a fork's pull request gets the checks only)
#   merge queue    ->  the checks again, on main with the queued pull requests merged onto it; no diffs
#   merge to main  ->  build the app, deploy dev (the site stack publishes the build), seed the catalog, tag a release
#   release        ->  "Deploy Production" takes it from there
#
# Production is reached only through a published release, so it always carries
# a version and has always already been to dev. One repository, one pipeline:
# the app and its hosting change together and go out together.
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      bump:
        description: Which part of the version to increment; auto reads the conventional commit titles since the last tag
        required: true
        default: auto
        type: choice
        options: [auto, patch, minor, major]
  pull_request:
    branches:
      - main
  # The merge queue builds a branch with the queued pull requests merged onto
  # main and asks for the same checks on it, so a pull request that went green
  # on a stale base is tested and diffed again as it will actually land.
  merge_group:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

env:
  NODE_VERSION: 22
  # CloudFront will not accept a certificate issued anywhere else, and one
  # region avoids a cross-region reference for the sake of one certificate.
  AWS_REGION: us-east-1
  GITHUB_ROLE_NAME: GitHubActionRole

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  Test:
=== DevDeploy job head ===
  # queue, on a fork's pull request, or on Dependabot's, is expected and
  # passes.
  Checks:
    name: Checks
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 5
    needs: [Test, InfraTest, Diff]
    if: ${{ always() && (github.event_name == 'pull_request' || github.event_name == 'merge_group') }}
    steps:
      - env:
          TEST: ${{ needs.Test.result }}
          INFRA: ${{ needs.InfraTest.result }}
          DIFF: ${{ needs.Diff.result }}
          EVENT: ${{ github.event_name }}
          SAME_REPO: ${{ github.event_name == 'merge_group' || github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository }}
          DEPENDABOT: ${{ github.actor == 'dependabot[bot]' }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          echo "Test: $TEST; hosting tests: $INFRA; diffs: $DIFF ($EVENT)"
          ok=true
          [ "$TEST" = "success" ] || { echo "::error::the app's checks did not pass ($TEST)"; ok=false; }
          [ "$INFRA" = "success" ] || { echo "::error::the hosting's checks did not pass ($INFRA)"; ok=false; }
          case "$DIFF" in
            success) ;;
            skipped) if [ "$EVENT" = "merge_group" ] || [ "$SAME_REPO" != "true" ] || [ "$DEPENDABOT" = "true" ]; then echo "The diffs were skipped here, as expected."; else echo "::error::the diffs did not run"; ok=false; fi ;;
            *) echo "::error::the diffs did not pass ($DIFF)"; ok=false ;;
          esac
          $ok

  DevDeploy:
    name: Deploy Dev
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 45
    # Restricted to main, so a deploy cannot be run from any other ref, and
    # holding the same secret names as the diff's environment.
    environment: deploy-dev
    permissions:
      contents: read
      id-token: write

You are implementing the final-review fix wave on branch `the-deck-drives` (HEAD 9c4bb4f). Every task on the branch passed its own review; a whole-branch review then found one Critical and eight Important findings at the seams between tasks. You own all of them in one pass. Work from C:\Users\xbox\ScrtGit\sbm-ui. Bash tool with POSIX syntax is available.

## What the branch does (one paragraph, so the findings make sense)

An outside client with no engine of its own attaches to the hosted WebSocket as a **deck** (`?token=<jwt>&as=deck`, `hosted/infra/lib/handlers/ws.ts`), is pushed `{ t: "runs" }` (runs a browser page is holding — a **writing connection**: signed in, not `control`, not `deck`; predicate `writes()`), watches one, and sends `{ t: "drive", run, seq, ref, press, move?, answer? }`. The server forwards it to writing connections; the page holding the run (`apps/web/src/run/RunView.tsx`, the drive effect ~line 447, using the pure `apps/web/src/run/takePress.ts`) checks `seq` against its `run.events.length`, presses the same `useRun` function its own button would, and replies `{ t: "drove", to, ref, ok, say? }`, which the server routes back to that deck. The page publishes what may be pressed as `offer` (`apps/web/src/run/offer.ts`, `offerOf`) beside its snapshot, gated on `publishing = shared || decks > 0`; `decks` comes from the server's `tools` gesture (`tellWhoIsAttached`), read by `useAttachedDecks`. The live store (`hosted/infra/lib/handlers/live.ts`, `dynamoLive`, and the `memoryLive()` double in `hosted/infra/test/ws.test.ts`) is two-row: a CONN row per connection, a watch row per (session, connection); `watchers(sessionId)` reads the watch rows. `scripts/drive.ts` is a headless proof and `docs/stream-api.md` documents the wire in a section "Driving a run from a deck".

Read the ledger's final-review block for context if you want it: C:\Users\xbox\ScrtGit\sbm-ui\.superpowers\sdd\2026-09-14-the-deck-drives-plan-a\progress.md (the lines beginning `- FINAL REVIEW`).

## The findings and the controller's ruling on each — implement exactly these

**C1 (Critical) — a press is applied once per device holding the run.** `ws.ts` (~477, 491): `writers` is every watcher passing `writes()`, and the press is posted to all of them — the owner's second device, and another member's browser, all apply it; the co-player's device then authors the event and its `drove` is dropped (~522, `target.sub !== conn.sub`). Ruling: (a) `live.ts` — the watch row stores the `at` that `watch()` already receives as `watchedAt`, `watchers()` returns `watchedAt` on each `Watcher`; `memoryLive` does the same. (b) `ws.ts` — `writers` = watchers passing `writes()` **and** `w.sub === conn.sub`, sorted newest `watchedAt` first (ties by `connectionId`), and **exactly one** is taken (`slice(0, 1)`). Tests: two pages of the owner watching → one `drive` posted, to the newer; a second member's page watching → nothing posted to it; the "no writer" refusal still fires when only another member holds the run.

**I2 — `moves` and `undo` escape the `live` gate.** `offer.ts` (~69-72): `bare` carries `moves`/`undo` into the `!live` return, and `takePress`'s `move`/`undo` arms consult only those. Ruling: the `!live` branch returns `moves: []`, `undo: null`, `primary: null`, `needsPage: "Open the run on the page"`. Test.

**I3 — per-contestant moves are offered and pressed against the table.** `RunView.tsx` (~283) maps every `run.moves`; the page's `Moves` (~2325) renders one button per contestant when `move.per === "contestant"` and a roster exists, calling `takeMove(id, label, undefined, contestant)`. Ruling: filter beside `heldMove` exactly as `Moves` splits — a `per === "contestant"` move is not offered when the run has contestants (read the JSX for the precise condition and mirror it). Test in `RunView.offer.test.tsx` if the fixture can carry a roster; otherwise a unit test of the extracted predicate plus a note.

# Finishing a Development Branch

## Overview

**Core principle:** Verify tests → Detect environment → Present options → Execute choice → Clean up.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the finishing-a-development-branch skill to complete this work."

## Step 1: Verify Tests

Run the project's full test suite (`npm test` / `cargo test` / `pytest` / `go test ./...`).

**If tests fail**, report the failures and stop — the menu comes after a green suite:

```
Tests failing (<N> failures). Must fix before completing:

[Show failures]
```

**If tests pass:** continue to Step 2.

## Step 2: Detect Environment

```bash
GIT_DIR=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
GIT_COMMON=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
# Capture now, while still inside the workspace — Step 5 changes directory
# before cleanup (Step 6) needs this value
WORKTREE_PATH=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)
```

This determines which menu to show and how cleanup works:

| State | Menu | Cleanup |
|-------|------|---------|
| `GIT_DIR == GIT_COMMON` (normal repo) | Standard 3 options | No worktree to clean up |
| `GIT_DIR != GIT_COMMON`, named branch | Standard 3 options | Provenance-based (see Step 6) |
| `GIT_DIR != GIT_COMMON`, detached HEAD | Reduced 2 options (no merge) | Externally managed — leave in place |

## Step 3: Determine Base Branch

The base branch is whatever this work forked from — usually named in the
plan, the conversation, or the branch's upstream. If it is not already
known, ask: "This branch split from <your best guess> - is that correct?"
Confirm before merging: merging into the wrong base is expensive to undo.

## Step 4: Present Options

**Normal repo and named-branch worktree — present exactly these 3 options:**

```
Implementation complete. What would you like to do?

1. Merge back to <base-branch> locally
2. Push and create a Pull Request
3. Keep the branch as-is (I'll handle it later)

Which option?
```

**Detached HEAD — present exactly these 2 options:**

```
Implementation complete. You're on a detached HEAD (externally managed workspace).

1. Push as new branch and create a Pull Request
2. Keep as-is (I'll handle it later)

Which option?
```

Present the menu exactly as written — concise, with every option coming
from the list above. Discarding the work happens only in response to your
human partner explicitly asking for it (see "If your human partner asks to
discard the work" below). Wait for their answer; the integration decision
is theirs.

## Step 5: Execute Choice

### Option 1: Merge Locally

```bash
# Get main repo root for CWD safety
MAIN_ROOT=$(git -C "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/.." rev-parse --show-toplevel)
cd "$MAIN_ROOT"

# Merge first — verify success before removing anything
git checkout <base-branch>
git pull
git merge <feature-branch>

# Verify tests on merged result
<test command>
```

If tests fail on the merged result: stop, leave the worktree and branch in
place, and investigate — nothing has been pushed, so the merge is local
and recoverable.

Once the merged result is green: clean up the worktree (Step 6), then
delete the branch:

```bash
git branch -d <feature-branch>
```

### Option 2: Push and Create PR

```bash
git push -u origin <feature-branch>
# From a detached HEAD, name the new branch on the remote:
# git push origin HEAD:refs/heads/<new-branch>
```

Then create the pull/merge request against <base-branch> with the forge's
tooling — its CLI if one is available, or the creation URL most forges
print when you push — following the repo's PR template and conventions if
present, and report the URL to your human partner.

Keep the worktree — your human partner iterates on PR feedback there.

### Option 3: Keep As-Is

Report: "Keeping branch <name>. Worktree preserved at <path>."

### If your human partner asks to discard the work

This path exists only as a response to an explicit request to throw the
work away. Confirm first:

```
This will permanently delete:
- Branch <name>
- All commits: <commit-list>
- Worktree at <path>

Type 'discard' to confirm.
```

Wait for that exact confirmation. When it arrives:

```bash
MAIN_ROOT=$(git -C "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/.." rev-parse --show-toplevel)
cd "$MAIN_ROOT"
```

Then clean up the worktree (Step 6) and force-delete the branch:

```bash
git branch -D <feature-branch>
```

## Step 6: Cleanup Workspace

**Runs for Option 1 and confirmed discards.** Options 2 and 3 always
preserve the worktree. Both callers have already changed directory to the
main repo root — worktree removal must run from outside the worktree —
and use the `GIT_DIR`/`GIT_COMMON`/`WORKTREE_PATH` values captured in
Step 2, from before that directory change.

**If `GIT_DIR == GIT_COMMON`:** Normal repo, no worktree to clean up. Done.

**If `WORKTREE_PATH` is under `.worktrees/` or `worktrees/`:** Superpowers
created this worktree — we own cleanup:

```bash
git worktree remove "$WORKTREE_PATH"
git worktree prune  # Self-healing: clean up any stale registrations
```

**If removal is refused** (`contains modified or untracked files`): the
worktree holds files that exist nowhere else — uncommitted plans, notes,
or scratch work. Never `--force` on your own initiative. Show your human
partner what is at stake and ask:

```bash
git -C "$WORKTREE_PATH" status --porcelain -uall
```

```
Worktree removal refused — these files were never committed:

<file list>

1. Commit them to <branch> before cleanup
2. Move them into <main repo root>
3. Delete them (unrecoverable)

Which?
```

Carry out the choice, then remove the worktree.

**Otherwise:** The host environment owns this workspace — leave it in
place. If your platform provides a workspace-exit tool, use it.

## Quick Reference

| Option | Merge | Push | Keep Worktree | Cleanup Branch |
|--------|-------|------|---------------|----------------|
| 1. Merge locally | yes | - | - | yes |
| 2. Create PR | - | yes | yes | - |
| 3. Keep as-is | - | - | yes | - |
| Discard (explicit request only) | - | - | - | yes (force) |

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Tests passed earlier this session" | Run the suite on the tree you are about to integrate. A green run only proves the tree it ran on. |
| "They obviously want it merged" | Integration is your human partner's decision. Present the menu and wait. |
| "They seem done with this feature — I'll offer to discard it" | The menu is complete as written. Discard happens only when your human partner asks for it in so many words. |
| "'Yeah, get rid of it' counts as confirmation" | Only the typed word `discard` authorizes deletion. |
| "The PR is up, so the worktree is clutter now" | PR feedback gets fixed in that worktree. It stays until the work lands. |
| "This other worktree looks stale — I'll clean it too" | Clean up only worktrees under `.worktrees/` or `worktrees/`. Everything else belongs to the host. |
| "Removal refused — `--force` is just finishing the cleanup" | The refusal means files exist only in that worktree. `--force` destroys them permanently. Show your human partner and ask. |
| "The merged-result failure is probably flaky" | A failing merged result stops everything. Branch and worktree stay put while you investigate. |
| "The base branch is obviously main" | Confirm the fork point or ask. Merging into the wrong base is expensive to undo. |
| "The push was rejected — force-push will fix it" | A rejected push means the remote moved. Investigate; force-push only on your human partner's explicit request. |

## Server

- `?token=<jwt>&as=deck` attaches a deck; `runs` is pushed on connect and whenever the set of runs held by a writing device changes.

- `drive` is forwarded to exactly one device: the owner's own, the one that watched the run most recently (`watchedAt`). `drove` is routed back to the deck that asked, with the run's new `seq`.

- One entitlement check and one feature parser (`billing.ts`), shared by both handlers; the live function now carries the gate's environment.

content.text:
Where things stand:

- **#288 merged and deployed to dev** (`Deploy Dev` succeeded; the run shows `waiting` only because "Tag and publish" waits on the release gate, by design).
- **A bug of mine surfaced on the first live attempt:** `scripts/drive.ts` renewed the CLI session but never saved the rotated one, so one run after the hour was up left your saved session dead — that's the "lapsed" you'd have hit on the next `runlog` command. **#289** fixes it (the script now goes through the CLI's own `bearer`, which renews and saves), auto-merge armed: https://github.com/SCRT-HQ/runlog/pull/289. This checkout already has the fix.

To run the proof I need two things from you, both quick:

```
npm run runlog -- login --api https://runlog.dev.scrthq.com/api
```

and a reload of the `streamdeck-test` tab so it's on the new site build. Say when, and I'll run the deck: list first, then one press with you watching.
I've reauthenticated the CLI. Shouldn't we be caching refresh tokens to prevent having to reauthorize the device, considering it's device flow?

Yes — and that's already how it works; the trip-up was my bug, not a missing cache. `runlog login` saves both tokens to the CLI's config file: the access token (one hour) and the refresh token (30-day inactivity on the CLI's WorkOS client). `bearer` renews silently when the access token is near expiry, and you never see the device flow again. What bit you is that WorkOS **rotates** the refresh token on every renewal — the old one is retired the moment the new one is issued — and my script renewed without writing the new pair back, so the file was left holding a dead token. With #289 the script saves what it renews, and one login should carry you for a month of use. Plan B's plugin keeps its own session file (`runlog-deck`, separate from the CLI's) for exactly this reason: two processes renewing one rotating token would race each other.

Now the proof. Server half first — no press, it just needs to be told which run you're holding:

content.text:
Plan A is complete, merged, deployed to dev, and proven against the real gateway. `main` is at `ecb2fc2` with all three PRs; the local branches were already pruned by the merge.

## What landed

| PR | Subject |
| --- | --- |
| #288 | `feat(live): a run can be driven from outside it` — 29 commits, 12 tasks, every one reviewed; one Critical and eight Importants from the whole-branch review fixed before merge |
| #289 | `fix(cli): the deck script keeps the session it renews` — found on the first live attempt |
| #290 | `fix(live): a deck is told its runs when it speaks, not at connect` — found on the second |

**Live on dev, tonight:** `hello` → `runs` in 270 ms · `watch` → the toast on your tab · a press with the doorbell's `seq` → `drove ok:true` with the new `seq` in ~600 ms and the run moved · a deliberately stale press → `"That moved on."` carrying the current `seq`. (Tell me what the tab did on that first press when you get a second — roll or enter — I'd like it in the record.)

## Rulings I made on your behalf

In order, each with what it costs if wrong. Everything here is reversible.

1. **Feature branch in the main working copy, not a worktree.** Your habit; nothing you haven't already accepted.
2. **No Claude trailers on any commit**, per your standing rule, over the harness's attribution guidance. A trailer can be added; a forbidden one can't be unpublished.
3. **A deck sends `watch` for the run it picked; the server re-writes its CONN row and tells the table.** Without it the page never learned a deck was on. One extra PUT per watch.
4. **Task 8 mirrors `needsPlus` exactly; `grantsOf` and `featuresFromEnv` extracted to `billing.ts`.** Same function, one spelling.
5. **Bus field `run`; `Acts.primary` dispatches on the offer's id** (roll → `begin`, carry-on → `completeStep`, close → `closeAndEnter`, enter → `enterUnit`). Caught by tests and the live run if wrong.
6. **`manual` with no checklist is a plain press; with items it needs the page; `finalizeUnit` with confirm items needs the page.** Hands-free's rule.
7. **`decksOf` tested on the memory double, not DynamoDB.** Same exposure as every other query in `live.ts`.
8. **`tellDecks`'s whole body inside one try** — a deck that can't be given its list is still connected. A swallowed store error shows as an empty picker, logged.
9. **The DynamoDB watch-row bug (Task 6's find) fixed in Task 7, with the test double made two-row-faithful.** Nil if wrong; it made the Task 4 test go red on its own.
10. **The live Lambda gets the gate env; one parser, not two.** One env var and one import.
11. **Between units, the offer carries "Enter Day N"; Finish stays on the page** (it's the Next/Finish fork, a decision). One input field.
12. **Task 9's three narrowings**: `close` routed by the engine's `closesUnit`, `answer` gated on a preset, held moves filtered; plus acts in try/catch and `seen` keyed by deck. Every change narrows a deck to what the page allows.
13. **Task 12 added mid-plan** for your tick-everything key, as a preset on a named key, never the follow key. One task; nothing downstream.
14. **The deck row lives in the `Attached` panel**, where tools are, not `Members`.
15. **`useToast` re-arms on identical text; one integration test for the note.** Nil.
16. **Off-list checklist rows are ticked tally-less, as the Constraints panel ticks them.** The tally arithmetic is proven against a real click.
17. **The headless script reads the CLI session and takes `seq` from the doorbell.** (Later corrected: it must *save* what it renews — #289.)
18. **Security review's "token in URL" flag acknowledged, no change** — it's the socket's existing contract; browsers and Node can't set the header.
19. **Final-review C1: one press lands on exactly one device — the owner's, newest `watchedAt`.** A press on the wrong one of your own devices is visible, not corrupting.
20. **`drove` carries the run's new `seq`, held until the log grows** (1500 ms fallback). Decided now so Plan B's follow key has it.
21. **Deferred with rulings, not fixed:** a page that leaves the run keeps its watch row (needs an unwatch on the wire); a retried `ref` waits on the timer; `tellWhoIsAttached` is chatty when a room reconnects; a future act's `TypeError` text could reach a key face.
22. **Kept the scratch workspace until the live check passed, then removed it.**
23. **A deck speaks first (`hello`); nothing ever posts from `$connect`.** Now a rule in memory.

## Not in the code, worth knowing

- `runlog login --api` wants the base **with** `/api` — that's what tripped your first login, and the CLI's error could say so.
- My shell's AWS profile isn't the dev account, so I couldn't read the live Lambda's log; not needed in the end.
- The main run for each merge sits at `waiting` on the release gate — that's "Tag and publish" waiting for its reviewers, by design.

## Next

Plan B — the plugin — is written at `.claude/plans/2026-09-14-the-deck-drives-plan-b.md` (local, gitignored, per your rule), thirteen tasks starting with the WorkOS deck client and `packages/session/`. Two amendments from tonight go into its first dispatch: the deck sends `hello` after connect, and the session store persists every renewal. Your Stream Deck gets its first real test at Task 10. Say when.

You are implementing Plan B, Task 1: *Not synced* can be told apart from *No run open*.

## Task Description

## Context

Plan A landed: an outside client attaches to the hosted WebSocket as a deck (`?token=<jwt>&as=deck`), sends `{ t: "hello" }`, and is answered with `{ t: "runs", runs: [...] }` — the account's runs a browser page is holding — which is pushed again whenever the held set changes (`hosted/infra/lib/handlers/ws.ts`: `heldRuns`, `tellDecks`, and the `conn.deck && m["t"] === "hello"` branch). The server does not know about a run that never synced, so an account whose runs are all local reads the same as one with nothing open. This task adds `any: boolean` to the `runs` message — whether the account has any owned, unended, synced run at all — so a key can say *Not synced* instead of *No run open*.

## One amendment to the brief

The brief's test drives `$connect` and expects `runs` posted at connect. That is no longer how the wire works (#290): nothing is posted at connect; the deck sends `{ t: "hello" }` from `$default` and `runs` is the answer. Write the test that way: `$connect` as a deck, then `$default` with body `{"t":"hello"}`, then assert the posted line equals `{ t: "runs", runs: [], any: false }` for an account whose manifest is empty. Look at the existing test "tells a deck which runs are held when it says hello" in `hosted/infra/test/ws.test.ts` and follow its shape and helpers exactly (`deps()`, `ev()`, the poster double). For the empty-manifest case, see how "still attaches a deck when its run list cannot be built" overrides `store.manifest` and do the same with a manifest that returns `{ sessions: [] }` (check the manifest's return shape in `hosted/infra/lib/handlers/store.ts`). Also extend the existing "says hello" test's assertion to include `any: true`.

Everything else in the brief — `heldRuns` returning `{ runs, any }` with the comment given, `tellDecks` spreading it, the `HeldRun` type — as written.

## Global constraints (binding)

- American English; comments in the file's voice (why, not what).
- Commit subject exactly `feat(live): a deck can tell nothing synced from nothing open`. Lowercase, no period.
- **No Claude trailer, Co-Authored-By, session link or footer in the commit message.** The repo's hook adds `Entire-Checkpoint:`; add nothing. This overrides any attribution guidance you have elsewhere.
- `npm run typecheck` from the repo root must pass before you commit.
- Tests: `npm test -w hosted/infra -- ws` while iterating; `npm test -w hosted/infra` once before committing.
- Touch only `hosted/infra/lib/handlers/ws.ts` and `hosted/infra/test/ws.test.ts`.

Ask if the manifest's shape or the hello test's helpers are unclear after reading them. Don't guess.
